dietEvidence.body: The dentition is consistent with carnivory. No gut contents are known; prey choice and hunting method are inferred from skull and postcranial anatomy.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: An early theropod from Antarctica with a transverse crest on the skull. The crest is preserved as bone; its display function is inferred.
summary: Cryolophosaurus ellioti is a theropod from the Hanson Formation of Antarctica, known from a partial skull and postcranial skeleton. It bears a prominent transverse crest on the skull. The Hanson Formation records a high-latitude, cool-temperate environment during the Early Jurassic.

discovery.body: Named by Hammer & Hickerson, 1994. The record is known from Hanson Formation, Transantarctic Mountains. A partial skull and postcranial skeleton from a high-latitude locality.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: A partial skull and postcranial skeleton from a high-latitude locality.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Hanson Formation, Transantarctic Mountains records the species in the Early Jurassic. The numeric range used here is ≈186–182 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Crest and skeleton
fossilEvidence.body: The skull bears a prominent transverse crest. The associated postcranium is incomplete but includes diagnostic material. Soft tissue is not preserved.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull has a distinctive transverse crest above the eyes, and the dentition is recurved and serrated.

behaviour.body: The transverse crest is usually interpreted as a display structure, but its function is not demonstrated. The animal lived in a seasonal, high-latitude environment; social behaviour and overwintering strategy are unknown.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from a partial skull and postcranial skeleton from a high-latitude locality. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The skull and postcranium are known from associated material, but the skeleton is incomplete. Crest function is inferred, and the high-latitude ecology is reconstructed from geology and flora.
